segs.text: Module four, objective three. Calculating creatinine clearance and what it means. The glomerular filtration rate, G F R, the volume of fluid the kidneys filter from the blood per unit time, shows how well a patient's kidneys are working. It is measured with a substance that is only filtered, neither secreted nor reabsorbed. Inulin is almost completely filtered, so it is the better marker, but it is not native to the body: it has to be given. Creatinine comes from the breakdown of muscle and is always in the blood, so creatinine clearance, C r C l, is the common clinical estimate of G F R. Creatinine is also secreted, which is why C r C l estimates G F R rather than measuring it.

card.m: GFR: the patient's renal function, mL/min
marker filtered only → its clearance = GFR
inulin: better marker, must be given
creatinine: from muscle, always present → CrCl
also secreted → an estimate of GFR

segs.text: The creatinine clearance estimate uses serum creatinine, S C r, the creatinine concentration in the blood in milligrams per deciliter, together with age, sex and ideal body weight, I B W. A higher serum creatinine gives a lower estimate, in inverse proportion, so twice the serum creatinine gives half the estimate. An older patient gets a lower estimate. A taller patient has a larger I B W, which raises the estimate. A woman's estimate is multiplied by zero point eight five, which rests on the assumption that women are smaller and less muscular than men. Serum creatinine may not reflect renal function well in people with unusually low or unusually high muscle mass. A normal C r C l is one hundred twenty to one hundred thirty milliliters per minute.

card.m: S<sub>Cr</sub> up → CrCl down; S<sub>Cr</sub> × 2 → CrCl × ½

segs.text: The Cockcroft-Gault equation says this: C r C l equals one hundred forty minus age, times I B W, over seventy two times S C r, times zero point eight five if female. Age is subtracted on the top, so each added year makes the top smaller, and serum creatinine sits on the bottom, so a larger value makes the result smaller. I B W multiplies the top, so a larger ideal weight raises the result. The units do not cancel, since the algebra gives kilograms over milligrams per deciliter, but the answer is reported in milliliters per minute. She said, I also want you to recognize that the units of creatinine clearance should be in milliliters per minute.

card.m: CrCl = {{frac:(140 − age) × IBW|72 × S<sub>Cr</sub>}}   (× 0.85 if female)
age in (140 − age): top smaller   S<sub>Cr</sub> on the bottom: result smaller
IBW on the top: result larger
{{frac:kg|mg/dL}}: units do not cancel; report mL/min

segs.text: I B W, in kilograms, comes from sex and height, and in this course it is always the weight used. For a male, I B W equals fifty plus two point three times the inches over five feet, and for a female, forty five point five plus two point three times the inches over five feet. The inches over five feet are the height in inches minus sixty. A height in centimeters is divided by two point five four, because one inch is two point five four centimeters, and a decimal height such as sixty four point five inches is read as written. Neither these lines nor Cockcroft-Gault are on the equation sheet. She said, this is an equation that I want you to know, to memorize.

card.m: IBW always; actual weight not used
inches over 5 ft = height in inches − 60

segs.text: Her slide example asks for the C r C l, using the ideal body weight, of a forty five year old woman who weighs sixty one kilograms, has a serum creatinine of one point one milligrams per deciliter, and is one hundred sixty five centimeters tall. Cockcroft-Gault answers it, and it needs the I B W first, so the height goes to inches: one hundred sixty five centimeters divided by two point five four is sixty four point nine six inches, which she rounds to sixty five, five inches over five feet. With the female line, forty five point five plus two point three times five, the I B W is fifty seven kilograms, and the sixty one kilogram actual weight is not used.

card.m: female, 45 yr, 61 kg, S<sub>Cr</sub> = 1.1 mg/dL, 165 cm

segs.text: In her slide example, Cockcroft-Gault takes the woman's age, forty five years, I B W, fifty seven kilograms, and serum creatinine, one point one milligrams per deciliter. The top, one hundred forty minus forty five, times fifty seven, is five thousand four hundred fifteen; the bottom, seventy two times one point one, is seventy nine point two. Their ratio is sixty eight point three seven, multiplied by zero point eight five because she is female. Her C r C l is fifty eight point one milliliters per minute. That is about half the normal one hundred twenty to one hundred thirty milliliters per minute, so her renal function is reduced. Working this example in class, a student answered fifty four, and she said that meant something had been done wrong.

What a patient's C r C l means for a drug. A low C r C l means a drug eliminated by the kidney is excreted more slowly and may accumulate, so depending on the drug, its dose may need adjusting. She named patients with a C r C l of thirty or sixty milliliters per minute as ones who will have trouble excreting such a drug. In a textbook example, renal function halves, so the drug's renal clearance halves from ten to five liters per hour, while its nonrenal clearance stays at five. Total clearance falls from fifteen to ten liters per hour, so the daily dose is lowered by a third to keep the same exposure.

card.m: CrCl low → renally eliminated drug excreted slower → may accumulate → adjust dose
e.g. (textbook) GFR halved: Cl<sub>R</sub> 10 → 5 L/hr, nonrenal 5 L/hr
Cl<sub>T</sub> 15 → 10 L/hr: daily dose down ⅓ for the same AUC

segs.text: How she tests it: a one patient vignette gives age, sex, height, often in centimeters, actual weight and serum creatinine, and the answer is in milliliters per minute. Sex decides two things, the I B W constant, fifty or forty five point five, and whether the zero point eight five applies. The trap she names herself is confusing the patient's creatinine clearance with a drug's renal clearance: C r C l describes the patient's kidneys, while a drug's renal clearance, from objective five, describes one drug and is compared with the average one hundred twenty milliliters per minute. Her review poll also keyed as false the claim that hepatic clearance is most readily approximated with creatinine clearance.

card.m: given: age, sex, height (cm), actual weight, S<sub>Cr</sub> → CrCl in mL/min
CrCl: the patient's kidneys   Cl<sub>R</sub>: one drug, compared with 120 mL/min
